entries.title: Germany says Russia behind attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport
entries.summary: Investigators believe an explosives-laden drone was deliberately targeting a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport in early August.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany blames Russia for attempted airport drone attack

September 1, 2026

Investigators believe an explosives-laden drone was deliberately targeting a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport in early August. The German government said on Tuesday that it held Russia "responsible."

The German government on Tuesday said Russia was "responsible" for an attempted drone attack at the Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4. 

"The federal government concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack in Leipzig," said Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt at a press conference in Berlin on Tuesday afternoon, adding that the attack fitted the pattern of a "long series of destabilization operations" against Europe.

Leipzig airport attack: What has Germany said?

"The means used — such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine," added Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul.

Authorities discovered a drone fitted with explosives and a detonation mechanism on the evening of August 4 in the security area of Leipzig/Halle Airport between Ukrainian cargo aircraft and believe a second drone may have collided with a DHL aircraft nearby.

Last week, German media reported a third drone, also loaded with explosives, had also been discovered at the airport. 

German federal prosecutors described the incident as a "serious attack on Germany's transport and logistics infrastructure."

"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," said Dobrindt.

"We do not view Leipzig as an isolated incident, but rather see it in the context of other hybrid actions. We assume that Germany will be the target of further hybrid attacks by Russia," he continued.

How will Germany respond?

Interior Minister Dobrindt insisted that Germany is "not at war" but that it is "a daily target of hybrid warfare." Therefore, he said, Germany would respond to the hybrid attack in Leipzig in a "proportionate and measured, yet resolute manner."

Foreign Minister Wadephul said Germany's response would be coordinated closely with European Union and NATO partners.

In addition to a strengthening of internal security, he also announced additional measures including the closure of the Russian consulate in the western city of Bonn from September 18 and the rescinding of a contract enabling the operation of the "Russian House," a Russian cultural center in Berlin.

EU top diplomat points finger at Russia

The European Union's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said earlier on Tuesday that it was "clear" that Russia was involved in the drone incident, but declined to comment further until Germany had identified those it believes were responsible,

Kallas said Russia was becoming increasingly provocative, raising the question of what could be done to deter Moscow from escalating tensions any further.

This is a developing story. Please refresh for updates.

entries.title: War and sanctions deepen Iran's fuel crisis
entries.summary: Long lines at fuel stations are spreading across Iran as war damage, import constraints and new US sanctions squeeze supplies.
entries.content:
Asia

War and sanctions deepen Iran's fuel crisis

September 1, 2026

Long lines at fuel stations are spreading across Iran as war damage, import constraints and new US sanctions squeeze supplies.

Only days after Washington announced a new round of economic sanctions on Iran, the country's gasoline shortage has become increasingly visible on the streets.  

In cities across Iran, drivers are reporting hours-long waits at filling stations. Videos circulating on social media show some people arriving before midnight or sleeping in their cars to secure fuel the following morning. Some stations have closed before serving everyone in line.

The situation is even more difficult for diesel. Truck drivers say queues at filling stations near major cities can stretch for kilometers, forcing them to wait overnight simply to obtain enough fuel to return to work.

Iran already faces a gasoline deficit of roughly 15 million liters a day. War damage, difficulties importing refined products and a tightening US blockade have made an old structural problem much harder to manage.

Hours in line for a few liters

A resident of Karaj, west of Tehran, told DW that some filling stations were limiting individual purchases to around five liters.

"I'm in the gasoline line right now. It took about 45 minutes just to get this far," he said. "Yesterday I went to several stations. Some were closed, some had no gasoline and others had very long queues."

He said he returned at 6 a.m. the next morning hoping to avoid the crowds but again found a long line.

He suspects the shortages are partly being used to prepare public opinion for higher gasoline prices, a claim that cannot be independently verified.

For truck drivers, waiting means losing income.

"Our whole life is either spent in the diesel line or on the road," one driver said. He described sleeping at a station while waiting for a tanker that might arrive around midday and supply only a few dozen trucks.

Another driver said he had been waiting since 8 a.m. after failing to obtain diesel the previous day.

For drivers whose earnings depend directly on keeping their vehicles moving, every lost day adds to rising insurance, tire, oil, repair and maintenance costs.

Is Iran changing its gasoline?

The shortage has coincided with the use of methanol in domestically produced gasoline.

Vahid Ghaneifard, chief executive of Persian Gulf Star Oil Company, recently confirmed that the refinery had begun testing methanol as an oxygenate in its gasoline.

The company says methanol makes up around 0.5% of the mixture. Iran's refining authorities say the national fuel standard permits methanol concentrations of up to 3%.

Officials insist the trial complies with technical requirements.

But the timing has fueled public suspicion.

Videos shared online show motorists holding bottles of unusually clear fuel and claiming that gasoline quality has deteriorated.

Some have alleged that water or excessive alcohol is being mixed into supplies. The allegations have not been independently corroborated.

There has, however, been at least one confirmed incident involving water contamination. In Rafsanjan, local authorities acknowledged that water had mixed with gasoline at a filling station after videos showed cars and motorcycles experiencing problems following refueling.

Officials said the incident resulted from a technical fault and was being investigated.

Distrust over fuel quality grows

For motorists already facing shortages, isolated incidents can reinforce wider fears.

A Tehran resident told DW he had spent about 1 billion tomans — roughly $5,250 (€4,529) at current exchange rates — repairing his car after its crankshaft failed. He believes poor-quality gasoline caused the damage, though such a connection has not been independently established.

He said he was reluctant to publicly protest.

Another resident in Rey, south of Tehran, told DW that motorists had gathered outside a filling station after several cars were allegedly damaged following refueling.

The concern is not simply technical, as it reflects a deeper collapse of trust between consumers and authorities at a time when the government is also discussing higher gasoline and diesel prices.

Tehran argues that the current subsidy system encourages excessive consumption and smuggling and imposes an unsustainable burden on state finances.

But consumers point to other issues such as inefficient cars, inadequate public transport and incomes that have failed to keep pace with inflation.

Is a price increase in the works?

Economist Hassan Mansour believes the government is once again preparing the political ground for higher energy prices.

Officials have repeatedly argued that Iranian gasoline prices are artificially low, that large volumes are smuggled abroad and that the economy consumes far more energy per unit of output than comparable countries.

The proposed solution is to bring domestic fuel prices closer to international levels.

"Once again, the government finds itself preparing the ground for raising the price of energy carriers," Mansour told DW.

But the problem runs deeper than subsidized gasoline.

Mansour points to the financial condition of Iran's oil industry. Budget documents indicate that the National Iranian Oil Company has tens of billions of euros in debt to the central bank and commercial banks, while the company also owes substantial sums to the National Development Fund and faces major tax liabilities.

When these debts cannot realistically be repaid, Mansour argues, they weaken state finances and contribute indirectly to currency instability and inflation.

Raising gasoline prices could therefore serve both as a demand-management measure and a source of additional revenue.

A politically dangerous choice

The government has few easy options.

While imports are harder to finance and transport, domestic production is struggling to keep pace with consumption.

Increasing output quickly requires investment and technology, while reducing consumption means either rationing fuel more aggressively or raising prices. Yet both carry political risks.

Iranian authorities remember what happened in November 2019, when a sudden gasoline price increase triggered nationwide protests followed by a deadly crackdown and an internet shutdown.

Today the economic environment is considerably more fragile.

War has damaged infrastructure, international sanctions are tightening and household purchasing power has fallen sharply. Long fuel queues are now adding another source of frustration.

For Tehran, raising prices might help reduce the gasoline deficit.

But doing so while people are already waiting overnight for fuel could turn an energy shortage into another crisis of public anger, which is something far more difficult to control.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: As glaciers melt, can communities be protected?
entries.summary: Rising temperatures are increasing the risk of floods and avalanches in mountain regions. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet shows the urgent need for solutions, and the tools that could help save lives.
entries.content:
September 1, 2026

Rising temperatures are increasing the risk of floods and avalanches in mountain regions. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet shows the urgent need for solutions, and the tools that could help save lives.

High mountain glaciers formed in the ice age are retreating and becoming unstable as the burning of fossil fuels heats the climate and leads to a decline in snowfall.



The instability creates the conditions for large glacial sections to collapse, triggering ice and rock avalanches that can dam river valleys before tidal waves of water are released.

Following the glacier collapse that triggered what is known as a mountain tsunami in Nepal and Tibet on August 26, thousands are still missing and feared dead. Unlike the 2025 glacier avalanche that destroyed the town of Batten in Switzerland — where nearly all inhabitants were evacuated — a lack of early warning systems in the Himalayas left locals and tourists at the mercy of flash floods.    

How much is climate change to blame?

The causes of glacier collapse are part of a complex web of interrelated changes to high mountain landscapes due in part to rising global temperatures, say scientists.

Levan Tielidze, research fellow in Glacial Geomorphology at Australia's Monash University, says the Himalayas are not, as is often imagined, a "frozen and relatively stable environment," but "dynamic systems in which glaciers, snow, permafrost, rock slopes, rivers and monsoon processes interact." 

"As the climate warms, these components are changing simultaneously, meaning hazards can cascade from one process into another," he tells DW. When rock, ice and water interact in more unpredictable ways on the world's highest peaks, the resulting debris flows "can transform into a catastrophic flood far downstream."

Almost 25 years ago, in what was then the biggest glacial collapse in history, one glacier crashed onto another in the Caucases Mountains of North Ossetia in the Russian Federation. The event caused avalanches of ice and debris that slid more than 24km (15 miles) and killed around 125 people.

"The Kolka Glacier disaster was one of the early warnings of the increasing occurrence and potential severity of such glacier-related hazards," Tielidze tells DW.

Meanwhile the UN says glaciers in Nepalese mountains have declined by one-third in 30 years, which has added to their instability.

Some research suggests that even if emissions from burning fossil fuels were low enough to prevent the planet from heating by more than 2 degrees Celsius (36 degrees Fahrenheit) compared to pre-industrial times, the wider Hindu Kush Himalayan region could lose up to half its glacier cover — compared to 2020 levels — by the end of the century.  

For Dipesh Chapagain, senior scientist at the United Nations University Institute for Environment and Human Security, there is "ample scientific evidence linking greenhouse gas emissions to global climate change, which in turn is driving glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and ice avalanches."   

"These changes are increasing both the frequency and intensity of climate-related disasters in mountain regions," he adds.

Chapagain has studied hundreds of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region — caused when meltwater from glaciers and snow creates a lake that eventually bursts and sends extreme flash floods downstream. The number of these events per decade has increased fivefold since the 1950s.  

The glacier collapse in Nepal and Tibet shares similarities to a GLOF event. However, the former was very different as it skipped the "intermediate lake-formation stage entirely … and directly triggered the flash flood," says Chapagain.

The avalanche also generated seismic activity equivalent to about magnitude 5.2 before the momentum of the water-rich debris flow that entered the river system saw it travel roughly 100 kilometres, notes Tielidze.

"These hazards are becoming so difficult to classify," he adds, in reference to the way mountain rock, ice and water are interacting in more unpredictable ways due to climate change.

Is it possible to adapt to more extreme glacier collapse impacts?

The 2025 glacial collapse in the Swiss Alps that destroyed the entire village of Blattan resulted in one fatality. Detailed surveillance of glacier deformation and the surrounding terrain allowed authorities to evacuate the population before the catastrophic collapse.

But this is less possible in the Hindu Kush Himalaya, which contains more than 63,700 glaciers, notes Tielidze.

"In the Himalayas, we need to move beyond monitoring only individual dangerous lakes," he says.

"We need integrated systems combining satellite observations, seismic detection, glacier and slope monitoring, river gauges, weather forecasts and automated warnings."

For rapidly evolving events such as the Nepal disaster, detecting seismic movement could give downstream communities "precious minutes of warning."

Chapagain says the transboundary nature of glacial hazards in the Himalayas makes "cross-border and regional cooperation on disaster preparedness" just as urgent as early-warning systems.

However, currently available adaptation technology and capacity may be insufficient to "respond to a disaster on the scale we've just witnessed on the Bhotekoshi River in Nepal." 

"What we have learned from this is we can adapt to climate change but not to climate apocalypse," says Shreya K.C., the Kathmandu-based advocacy working group co-coordinator of the Loss and Damage Youth Coalition, in a statement.

A rapid reduction in planet-heating emissions that are at driving glacial melt and instability will need to accompany any adaptation measures.

"We cannot engineer our way out of unlimited warming," says Tielidze. "Some mountain hazards will remain unpredictable and some changes will eventually exceed the capacity of communities and infrastructure to adapt."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: Mladic's death, Bosnia and Serbia's unfinished reckoning
entries.summary: The death of Ratko Mladic did not close a dark chapter of European history; it reopened old wounds. The ideology that created him lives on. The Dayton peace agreement ended the war, not the divisions that produced it.
entries.content:
Bosnia and Herzegovina

Mladic's death, Bosnia and Serbia's unfinished reckoning

September 1, 2026

The death of Ratko Mladic did not close a dark chapter of European history; it reopened old wounds. The ideology that created him lives on. The Dayton peace agreement ended the war, not the divisions that produced it.

The death of Ratko Mladic should have closed one of the darkest chapters in European history.

Instead, it has reopened old wounds, proving that both the Dayton Accords that ended the 1992-95 Bosnian war and the three decades of international engagement that followed never came close to addressing the causes that led to the conflict.

When Mladic, the former commander of the Bosnian Serb army, died on August 27, 2026 in a prison hospital in The Hague, his conviction for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes — including the 1995 Srebrenica massacre and the siege of Sarajevo — had been final for nearly a decade.

What was never settled, however — and what, it seems, was never even seriously attempted — is the question of how a society lives with a man who remains a convicted criminal in the eyes of an international court but is viewed by some as a hero and symbol of the Serbian people.

For this reason, the reactions that followed Mladic's death came as no surprise.

Mladic openly mourned in Republika Srpska

In Serbia and the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska, one of the two semi-autonomous entities created within Bosnia-Herzegovina by the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, Mladic's death was mourned as the loss of a national hero, not the end of an era of crimes — a narrative that stands in direct contradiction to the facts established by international courts.

Senior officials in Republika Srpska, which covers around 49% of the territory of the former Yugoslav republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, called on citizens to gather in squares and light candles "for the salvation of the general's soul."

Milorad Dodik, still the most powerful political figure in Republika Srpska despite stepping down as its president last year after a six-year ban on holding public office imposed by Bosnia's constitutional court, called Mladic's death a "murder," suggesting it was "an organized approach that was meant to lead to a fatal outcome."

In Banja Luka, the de facto capital of Republika Srpska, Mayor Drasko Stanivukovic expressed his condolences to Mladic's family and confirmed that Mladic is not perceived as a man convicted of genocide but as a symbol of "a time and a struggle."

Institutional support in Belgrade

In the Serbian capital, Belgrade, this stance received institutional backing.

Serbia's justice minister announced a funeral with the highest state and military honors.

President Aleksandar Vucic accused the tribunal in The Hague of "uncivilized behavior" for not allowing Mladic to spend his final days outside his prison cell.

Former Interior Minister Aleksandar Vulin spoke of Mladic in the same breath as other Serbian national heroes, invoking a narrative linking World War I to the 1990s, saying, "From Gavrilo Princip to Ratko Mladic, the best Serbs are killed tied up."

A very different response elsewhere in Bosnia

In the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the other main entity in Bosnia, where Bosniaks and Croats form the majority, news of Mladic's death was met with unanimous condemnation of the deceased, given that Mladic was finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, a town in eastern Bosnia where around 8,000 men and boys were killed in July 1995.

Bosnia's foreign minister, Elmedin Konakovic, framed the official Serbian response as Serbia's conscious choice. "No one is forcing Serbia to treat Mladic as a hero, nor to attribute his crimes to it. Serbia is choosing this itself," he said.

Representatives of victims and survivors pointed out that any public glorification is a direct insult to the families of those killed.

The European Commission, responding to questions about the announced state funeral, said that "glorifying convicted war criminals is contrary to the most basic European values" and that such practices have no place in either member states or candidate countries.

The European Movement in Serbia warned that a state funeral would amount to "institutional glorification" and a "serious moral, legal and political attack on Serbia." It urged the Serbian government to abandon the plan.

How can this happen?

But how is it possible that a man who has been finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica is still honored as a military commander?

The answer is not simply that he is viewed by some as a national hero. It is structural, and it begins with the Dayton peace agreement itself.

The 1995 Dayton Accords ended the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina by turning existing front lines and territorial control into the constitutional architecture of a new state.

One of the fundamental elements of the agreement was Republika Srpska, which is recognized by all signatories and embedded in the constitutional structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

That division was not an administrative technicality; it reflected the political reality on the ground at the time negotiations were held, including territories under the control of forces commanded by Mladic.

The compromise was necessary to stop the bloodshed. The problem is that since 1995, it has never been accompanied by a mechanism for dealing with the past that would match the political compromise.

Dayton created a complex constitutional architecture — a state divided into two entities and the Brcko District with a total 14 governments and parliaments at state, entity and cantonal level — for a country of just 3 million people.

It is a system built to prevent war, not a system built to produce common citizenship, and was described by the Council of Europe's Venice Commission as long ago as 2005 as "neither rational nor efficient."

In such a system, where ethnic identity is built into the very logic of power, denial or relativization of crimes is not a marginal phenomenon, it is a political resource.

In other words, each side sees itself as a victim, which makes joint recognition of committed evil as a precondition for reconciliation impossible.

Price of missed responsibility

Bosnia-Herzegovina has state-level legislation that criminalizes the public denial, gross minimization or justification of genocide and the glorification of persons convicted of such acts.

In reality, however, enforcement of this legislation remains uneven.

Serbia has no such law, and its public authorities, instead of distancing themselves from Mladic's legacy, openly embrace it.

This is not just a symbolic difference, it is the difference between treating the wartime legacy as something shameful to be overcome or as a resource to be politically exploited.

Dayton Accords helped maintain status quo

The international community, which stopped the war in 1995 through force and diplomacy, has subsequently retreated into the role of administrator of the status quo.

The Office of the High Representative, the international envoy empowered to impose laws and remove obstructive politicians under the Dayton Accords, did indeed impose laws and remove obstructive politicians for decades. But in doing so it only stabilized the system without dismantling its causes.

The result is twofold: a deeply divided society that has not moved forward in the 30 years since the end of the war, and the fact that an ideology that gave rise to that war is still very much alive.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

entries.title: Will Bangladesh join the Mecca defense alliance?
entries.summary: While Bangladesh is weighing the risks of signing the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, experts warn that such a move could complicate relations with neighboring India.
entries.content:
Bangladesh

Will Bangladesh join the Mecca defense alliance?

September 1, 2026

While Bangladesh weighs the risks of signing the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, experts warn that such a move could complicate relations with neighboring India.

There has been widespread speculation about Bangladesh becoming part of a mutual defense deal struck last month by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. But the South Asian country says it has yet to receive an invitation.

The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, ​signed into force in early August, ​is intended to strengthen collective ​deterrence against any act of aggression. It stipulates that an ​armed attack against any of the three countries would be regarded ​as an attack on all.

Some analysts believe the pact has already changed the geopolitical landscape of the Middle East and South Asia.

"Although it is a collective defense understanding, from a strategic perspective it is primarily an initiative to maintain the regional balance of power and advance the respective interests of the participating states," ​Navine Murshid, a political science and sociology professor at North South University in Dhaka, told DW.

Mecca pact and Bangladesh-India factor

Any move by Bangladesh to join, however, could complicate its foreign relations, particularly with neighboring India.

The two countries share a 4,096-kilometer (2,545-mile) land border, and have strong cultural and economic ties.

India, a fierce rival of Pakistan, sheltered many Bangladeshi refugees and provided military support to Bangladesh during its independence war against Islamabad in 1971.

However, ties between New Delhi and Dhaka have become increasingly contentious since a deadly student-led uprising in 2024 toppled then Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who was considered a close ally of the Indian government.

Now living in exile in India, Hasina has since been convicted in absentia for crimes against humanity during the uprising. She has denied the charges.

Bangladesh's current government, headed by the center-right Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), is in favor of the Mecca agreement.

"We view this pact positively," Bangladeshi Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman said in response to a question in parliament last week.

But he insisted that the question of Bangladesh joining the pact, or even considering membership, had not yet arisen, as that would depend on the intentions of its current members.

"If they express an intention to include Bangladesh in the pact, we will certainly consider it positively," he said.

When asked about the remarks made by Bangladeshi officials, India said the pact had implications for its national security and that it was closely monitoring the situation.

"We continue to follow all developments that have a bearing on India's security and take all necessary steps to safeguard it," Randhir Jaiswal, a spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs, told reporters in New Delhi last week.

Competing geopolitical interests

Analysts say Dhaka needs to consider its interests carefully before making any move to join the joint defense pact.

"The scope for direct conventional interstate war or military conflict in South Asia is limited. Therefore, the primary role of such an agreement is not confined to conducting border wars," Murshid said.

"In international relations, its significance lies mainly in strengthening bargaining power and maintaining one's position against the influence of other regional countries."

Murshid added that Pakistan's interest in bringing Bangladesh closer through this agreement "is driven by geographical and political considerations."

"For India, the security of the Siliguri Corridor and its eastern frontier are important considerations. If Pakistan's defense-related influence in Bangladesh were to increase, New Delhi could view this as a development capable of affecting the regional balance of relationships," he said.

In such circumstances, Bangladesh would have to clearly define what it would and would not do by joining this alliance, she explained.

"In particular, a clear position would be necessary regarding Bangladesh's role if a military conflict were to arise between India and Pakistan. Taking Pakistan's side during such a conflict could create political and diplomatic pressures for Dhaka that may exceed Bangladesh's capacity to manage," she stressed.

Dhaka-based former diplomat M Humayun Kabir sees no reason for Bangladesh to join the pact. "Bangladesh has not joined any military alliance over the past 50 to 55 years. As far as I am concerned, I believe that position remains unchanged to this day," he told DW.

"They are talking about a regional security arrangement, but the region in question concerns Pakistan and the Middle East. We are not part of that region or geographical area. Bangladesh is located in the eastern part of South Asia. Therefore, there is no direct geographical rationale for Bangladesh to participate in such a military alliance," he added.

Will Bangladesh benefit from joining the pact?

Murshid stressed that Bangladesh needed to develope its own defense infrastructure and security systems sustainably.

She believes becoming part of an international security agreement could help modernize Dhaka's defense capabilities and facilitate access to military technology.

"The text of the agreement does not directly mention trade, labor markets, or economic relations. However, it is natural for economic elements to become linked with a security framework, a phenomenon known in international relations as issue linkage," she told DW.

However, Kabir fears joining the pact could limit Bangladesh's geopolitical options and recommended a balanced approach. "We contribute to peacekeeping missions around the world under the auspices of the United Nations, and that is important to us. Our economy is interconnected with many different countries in various ways, which is also important. Our workforce is present in countries across the world, and that, too, is an important consideration," he told DW.

"Therefore, before making any decision on this issue, we must take into account the many different dimensions and forms of our national interests."

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Norway's new King Haakon VIII takes oath in parliament
entries.summary: The new king swore to uphold the constitution in parliament in Oslo, the first major institutional step of his reign. Haakon VIII's wife Queen Mette-Marit had to skip the event in the aftermath of her lung transplant.
entries.content:
Norway

Norway's new King Haakon VIII takes oath in parliament

September 1, 2026

The new king swore to uphold the constitution in parliament in Oslo, the first major institutional step of his reign. Haakon VIII's wife Queen Mette-Marit had to skip the event in the aftermath of her lung transplant.

New King Haakon VIII swore an oath of allegiance to Norway's consititution in the parliament in Oslo on Tuesday, following him succeeding his father Harald V, who died last week. 

This follows a day after Harald's coffin was taken to the chapel of the royal palace, where it will remain for the public to pay their last respects until a funeral on September 9.

What happened in the parliamentary ceremony?

Haakon was driven the short distance from the royal palace to the Storting, or parliament in Oslo.

House speaker Masud Gharahkhani read the official announcement of Harald's death and Haakon's succession before the new constitutional monarch took the oath.

"I promise and swear that I will govern the Kingdom of Norway in according with its constitution and laws, so help me god, the almighty and omniscient," the 53-year-old said.

Queen Mette-Marit skips event amid complications following lung transplant

Ahead of he ceremony, the palace said that Haakon's wife Queen Mette-Marit would not be attending.

She had made her first public appearance since assuming the title on Monday in the coffin procession but is recovering after a lung transplant in June.

In a statement, the palace quoted Are Holm, a pulmonologist at Oslo's University Hospital, as saying that complications following a transplant are not uncommon and that Mette-Marit had experienced them on several occasions, including Tuesday.

"As a result, the Queen must remain under observation throughout the day. Unfortunately, the Queen will therefore be unable to attend the swearing-in ceremony at the Storting today," he said.

What's the role of Norway's largely symbolic monarchy?

Norway's royal family can trace its roots bak to the ninth century.

When the country regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters supported the idea of reinstating a largely symbolic constitutional monarchy in a plebiscite.

Most political power lies with the elected government and parliament, but Norway's royals retain a predominantly soft power role in diplomacy and promoting the country around the world.

entries.title: Germany's center-left SPD is fighting for survival
entries.summary: The Social Democratic Party is sinking ever deeper into crisis. Voters are turning away, while unrest is growing within its grassroots ranks. Will upcoming state elections accelerate the party's downward spiral?
entries.content:
Germany

Germany's center-left SPD is fighting for survival

September 1, 2026

The Social Democratic Party is sinking ever deeper into crisis. Voters are turning away, while unrest is growing within its grassroots ranks. Will upcoming state elections accelerate the party's downward spiral?

At a fitness class run by the Workers' Welfare Association, one stop on his tour through Saxony-Anhalt, Matthias Miersch is giving it his all: Hands up, hands down, touch your toes, all in time to the German schlager hit "Regenbogenfarben."

Miersch, leader of the center-left Social Democratic Party's (SPD) parliamentary group, has traveled to Saxony-Anhalt for a 24-hour visit to lend his support.

The election campaign in the eastern German state has entered its decisive final phase. In the state capital, Magdeburg, and three smaller towns, Miersch meets with SPD state politicians and local residents. He takes part in discussions with a queer advocacy organization, a housing cooperative and an initiative dedicated to the social integration of young refugees.

Everything revolves around the party's core issues: affordable housing, social support, poverty reduction, integration and protection against discrimination based on sexual identity. At the Rainbow Cafe in Magdeburg, Miersch speaks openly about his own sexual identity as a gay man. Those gathered there describe the open hatred and hostility they encounter, especially in rural areas, and speak of their growing fear of the prospect of a state government led by the Alternative for Germany (AfD).

The AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch has been classified by the domestic intelligence agency as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization.

"We are witnessing a rollback of the freedoms and lifestyles that have emerged over recent decades," Miersch said at the cafe. The small room is colorful and crowded; a nearby shelf is decorated with small flags bearing the slogan "No Time for Nazis."

SPD cannot stop the AfD

The Social Democrats have little with which to counter the AfD's rise in Saxony-Anhalt. Germany's oldest political party is polling at just 7 to 8%, compared to the AfD's 42%.

The SPD's main concern is that it might even fall below the 5% threshold for representation in parliament. The reason for the dwindling support is that many voters feel the party — the junior coalition partner in the deeply unpopular federal government alongside the center-right Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) — no longer has a clearly defined identity.

"I do not want to conceal the fact," Miersch told journalists traveling with him at the end of the tour, "that federal politics is also fueling debate here on the ground."

What he is referring to above all is the planned reform of the statuary pension system, especially the proposal to abolish the option of early retirement after 45 years, often referred to as retirement at 63. For many residents of Saxony-Anhalt, which has long grappled with an aging population and demographic decline, the proposal is a particularly contentious issue.

Elections in five federal states

Yet Saxony-Anhalt is not the only place where the SPD is battling decline. Nationwide, the party is polling at only around 12%, trailing the AfD, the CDU/CSU and the Greens.

The situation is even more acute in some individual states. With elections in five of Germany's 16 states and city-states, 2026 is a super election year. Two of those contests have already taken place.

The results so far are sobering: in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg, the SPD recorded its worst result of the postwar era and only just managed to retain its representation in the state parliament. In Rhineland-Palatinate, after 35 years in power, the party was decisively pushed into second place by the CDU. Its election result there was the worst in the state's history.

September now threatens to bring further setbacks, and not only in Saxony-Anhalt. In the city-state of Berlin, the party is languishing in fifth place at just 12%, while in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania it could face the same fate as in Rhineland-Palatinate: a loss of power.

Frustration growing within SPD

An increasing number of Social Democrats are speaking of an existential crisis. The once-proud workers' party, which at its peak could count every second voter among its supporters, now faces the prospect of political irrelevance.

"I see a party that is dying," Berlin state legislator Orkan Özdemir, co-chair of the SPD's Working Group on Migration and Diversity, told the German Press Agency in early August.

In a letter to the party executive, the group's leadership called for a special party conference this autumn and a restructuring of the party leadership. They are far from alone in doing so.

Dissatisfaction, which first surfaced after the SPD's initial two state election defeats, is now spreading throughout the party. This comes at a particularly difficult moment, with the SPD in the midst of an election campaign and, in principle, expected to project unity.

Painful compromise over social, migration policies

At the heart of the criticism is the dual role of party leaders Bärbel Bas and Lars Klingbeil, who also serve as members of the federal government. Critics argue that the arrangement is simply not working. 

As labor minister and finance minister, respectively, they are seen as doing too little alongside CDU Chancellor Friedrich Merz to give the SPD a distinct political profile of its own.

Too many concessions, particularly on social policy, have been made to the CDU, critics contend: cuts to housing benefits, the abolition of Germany's "retirement at 63" provision, and the requirement to provide a doctor's note from the first day of illness.

The party is also facing headwinds over its tougher migration policy. Those calling for a special party conference argue that a long-overdue debate is needed over whether the government's course still reflects the party's own principles and policy positions.

Challenge for party leaders Bas, Klingbeil

The question of what the SPD still stands for, whom it represents and what it should support in the future is increasingly becoming a matter of the party's very survival.

"We have lost the trust of voters because, on many issues, the SPD was unwilling to ruffle feathers," Bas said after the first two state elections this year. "In some cases, we have also failed to communicate clearly. Many people no longer know what the SPD stands for."

Klingbeil has also expressed understanding for the critics, though he remains unfazed. It is perfectly normal for issues to be debated within the party, he said during a campaign appearance in Saxony-Anhalt.

"We're at 12% nationwide, and these are extraordinarily turbulent times. I know that some of the decisions made at the federal level are demanding a great deal from my own party, too," he said.

Workers voting for the AfD

According to an analysis by the polling institute Forsa published in November 2025, only 9% of blue-collar workers and unemployed voters would now choose the SPD. Those who feel socially disadvantaged today are increasingly drawn to the AfD. In February 2025, pollsters at infratest dimap published figures showing that 38% of workers were voting for the AfD.

For the SPD, that is a sobering finding.

More and more Social Democrats see their party at a turning point. They are calling on the SPD to find its way back to a clearly recognizable political profile, if necessary even from the opposition benches.

Otherwise, they fear, the party could be crushed between the demands of governing, internal factional struggles and the loss of its former core electorate.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Nepal flood: Death toll tops 1,000 as rescue continues
entries.summary: Nepalese authorities say 4,000 people remain unaccounted for as rescue teams with search dogs comb through mud, rocks and debris.
entries.content:
September 1, 2026

Nepalese authorities say 4,000 people remain unaccounted for as rescue teams with search dogs comb through mud, rocks and debris.

The death toll after a massive flash flood last week at the Himalayan border between Nepal and China has risen more than 1,000 people, local authorities said on Tuesday.

In Nepal, 987 deaths have already been reported, with almost 4,000 people still being unaccounted for. In China,16 deaths and 546 missing people have been reported. 

The list of missing people includes some 800 foreign nationals.

Search and rescue teams are still carrying out operations despite difficult conditions and unstable terrain.

Search dogs are also taking part in the search efforts through mud, rocks and debris the flash floods left behind.

Roads were destroyed in places, cutting off access.

Efforts are also being made to locate the some 500 workers believed to be trapped inside the tunnels of twelve hydropower project tunnels, according to Nepalese authorities.

Climate change raises risk for region, PM says

The flash floods on August 28, started as a glacial collapse in the Himalayas triggered a powerful stream of rock, ice and meltwater into the valleys below.

The stream was so powerful that a seismic event of 5.2 magnitude was recorded.

Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah reacted to the disaster by emphasizing the need to fight climate change.

"This incident has indicated that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing with climate change," he posted on social media.

"Therefore, this region must be alert, and at the same time, it is time for us to strongly raise the issue of disasters caused by climate change before the international community."

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: US irks Germany, Europe with Russian G20 invite, press bans
entries.summary: Russia's finance minister is at the G20 meeting in Asheville but some key US press corps members are not. The mood was already tense amid the lengthy Iran war and Trump's renewed beef with neighbor Canada.
entries.content:
United States of America

US irks Germany, Europe with Russian G20 invite, press bans

September 1, 2026

Russia's finance minister is at the G20 meeting in Asheville but some key US press corps members are not. The mood was already tense amid the lengthy Iran war and Trump's renewed beef with neighbor Canada.

G20 finance ministers and central bank heads gathered in Asheville, North Carolina for two days of talks.

The session is being overshadowed by dissatisfaction over the White House welcoming Russia to the meeting but not some critical reporters, the war with Iran and its economic fallout, and Donald Trump's latest trade dispute with Canada. 

Who is representing Russia at the meeting?

Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov made an unexpected appearance as talks opened late on Monday. He held a bilateral meeting with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

"We like getting along with everybody," Trump told reporters when asked about the first in-person Russian invite since the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. 

The US currently holds the rotating G20 presidency and so is hosting the session.

The US government told several news agencies on condition of anonymity that Bessent used the meeting to tell Siluanov that the US would not give Russia economic relief until it brings its four-and-a-half-year invasion to a close.

How did European delegates respond?

"Receiving the Russian finance minister here sends a troubling signal," German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said. 

He said he and his European colleagues made clear that they would not appear in the traditional "family photo" alongside the Russian media, saying this was a common EU position.

The photo was ultimately taken without Siluanov and away from the media.

Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski told the Reuters news agency that he recognized the right of the G20 hosts to invite guests, but that he was unhappy to see Moscow represented.

"We do not trust Russia. They lie constantly and you need to be really, really cautious while discussing with them," he said. "So for me it would be very difficult to have any kind of conversation with Russia."

Which reporters and outlets were excluded?

As leaders gathered in Asheville, three giants of the US media landscape complained of either no or limited access to the meeting.

The business-focused Bloomberg News said that its team was not allowed access, while the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times both complained that certain journalists who would typically cover such events were refused media credentials.

Following a challenge from the DJV German journalists' union on Monday, Klingbeil was critical on the matter.

"I believe the press has a completely legitimate interest in reporting openly and freely on this G20 summit," he said. "I consider it unacceptable for journalists or entire editorial teams to be excluded."

Intractable Iran war weighing down global economy

Klingbeil had also said in a German political podcast last week that he would bring a simple message to the US regarding what he called Donald Trump's "irresponsible" war in Iran — that it needed to come to an end. 

Host Bessent, however, was trying to drum up support among allies for the US plans for what it calls "Operation Economic Outcast," an intensified sanction regime against Iran reliant in no small part on third parties outside the US who still do business with Tehran.

Iran has withstood decades of extensive US and western sanctions, but Bessent tried to argue when asked by reporters that it could swiftly be made to collapse if its remaining trading partners joined in.

"I think it could be within weeks or months — and the economy doesn't have to collapse, we just have to have the regime come to their senses," he said.

Trump's latest Canada meltdown unsettles allies

The other major source of strain at the meeting was last week's sudden deterioration in trade talks between the US and Canada.

This quickly descended into the tit-for-tat imposition of tariffs, and President Trump launching various social media jabs before unilaterally redesignating Lake Ontario as Lake America, at least on the books in the US. 

Canada's Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne sought to stress that even the recent friction did not impact his participation.

"Canada has always been at the table and constructive, ready to discuss," he told reporters, stressing the need to ensure continued economic growth and "bring back some stability in trade."

entries.title: Germany news: Explosive devices found near power plant
entries.summary: Police say they found unconventional explosive and incendiary devices near the Jänschwalde power plant in Brandenburg. Meanwhile, Germany's top diplomat says Algeria could become an important supplier of gas.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Explosive devices found near power plant

Published September 1, 2026last updated September 1, 2026

Police say they found unconventional explosive and incendiary devices near the Jänschwalde power plant in Brandenburg. Meanwhile, Germany's top diplomat says Algeria could become an important supplier of gas.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Police say they have found explosive devices near a power plant in Brandenburg
  • Germany's Foreign Minister Wadephul in Algeria for talks on renewable energy and gas
  • Wadephul stressed the need to "diversify" energy sources, describing Algeria as a "reliable partner"
  • The top diplomat also vowed a measured response to an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport last month
  • IG Metall union chief says Volkswagen is making a "big mistake" by mulling further job cuts and plant closures

Welcome to our roundup of news and analysis from and concerning Germany on Tuesday, September 1.

Tired of missing our real time updates? Click here  to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google. 

Skip next section Officials: 'attempted attack' on power grid outside of Berlin

Officials: 'attempted attack' on power grid outside of Berlin

German authorities have released more details about a suspected attack on an electric power station in the eastern German state of Brandenburg.

Police found several homemade explosive devices near the electrical substation in Turnow-Preilack, southeast of Berlin. Local network operator 50Hertz described the devices as small rockets resembling New Year’s Eve fireworks.

Some of the devices had been launched while others were found unexploded, the operator said. There was a brief power cut, but all power ‌lines are back in operation

The Turnow-Preilack substation is where the electricity from the Jänschwalde power plant is distributed across the region.

Brandenburg State Premier Dietmar Woidke called it an "attempted attack" and condemned the act. "The worryingly high frequency of such incidents shows that we must decisively protect our infrastructure," he said.

The suspected sabotage follows a series of recent strikes on the power grid around Berlin.

In January, an arson attack by suspected far-left extremists on power lines in left 45,000 households in the German capital without electricity for days.

In March 2024, another group targeted an electricity pylon, cutting power to a Tesla factory outside of Berlin.

Skip next section Germany's Antonio Rüdiger retires from international football

Germany's Antonio Rüdiger retires from international football

German central defender Antonio Rüdiger has announced his retirement from international football, saying he wanted to "clear the path for the younger generation" after the 2026 World Cup exit. 

"When I first wore the German jersey in 2014, even in my dreams I couldn't have pictured going on to play 86 national team games," Rüdiger said in a post on Instagram. 

"Even though the big prizes eluded us in recent competitions and we had to stomach some painful defeats, this was still an extremely special chapter for me that will have a lasting impact," Rüdiger said.

The 33-year-old Real Madrid defender, who rose the ranks with Stuttgart and also had spells with Roma and Chelsea, was extremely unfortunate with the timing of his Germany career.

He made his debut in May 2014 in the preparations for what would become Germany's fourth World Cup win, but narrowly missed the cut for the tournament proper that summer.

Over the next 12 years he established himself as a regular in the squad and then in the starting 11. But this coincided with a dry spell where the German team only won the 2017 Confederations Cup and endured three consecutive early World Cup exits — twice in the group stages and most recently in the first knockout round against Paraguay this summer. 

Skip next section Berlin Pride memorial bench destroyed

Berlin Pride memorial bench destroyed

A bench meant to commemorate the deadly Berlin Pride attack has been destroyed, authorities said. 

The rainbow bench at the site of the July 25 attack has been vandalized "with considerable physical force," local police said.

Berlin's queer commissioner, Alfonso Pantisano, said he was shocked after seeing photos of the damage.

The original attack occurred when a 21-year-old Islamist extremist drove a van into a crowd at the Berlin Pride event and then attacked people with a machete.

One woman from Poland was killed, and 31 others were injured, some seriously, before police fatally shot the attacker the following day.

The bench was placed next to a newly planted tree that replaced one destroyed during the attack.

Local authorities have said it will be rebuilt and have filed a criminal complaint against unknown perpetrators.

Skip next section Prosecutors charge 2 suspected members of German right-wing terror group

Prosecutors charge 2 suspected members of German right-wing terror group

The Federal Public Prosecutor's Office has brought charges against two suspected members of the violent far-right Last Wave of Defence group for planning to set fire to an asylum seekers' facility.

The pair are accused of traveling to the accommodation center in Schmölln in central Germany in January 2025 with the intention of setting it on fire. They allegedly smashed windows but failed to set the building alight. 

The two suspects, aged 16 and 17 at the time of the incident, were arrested at the end of June.

They have been charged with aiding and abetting attempted murder, attempted arson resulting in death, and attempted aggravated arson.

The Thuringia Higher Regional Court in Jena must now decide whether they will stand trial.

According to the prosecutor's office, one of the two is currently being held in pre-trial detention.

Last month, a court in Hamburg sentenced seven young members of the terror group to prison terms ranging from one and a half to five years.

Skip next section Merz: No coalition, but some kind of interplay with Left Party possible in Saxony-Anhalt

Merz: No coalition, but some kind of interplay with Left Party possible in Saxony-Anhalt

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has expanded on how he hopes a CDU-led coalition — presumably without a clear majority — could still govern in Saxony-Anhalt after Sunday's elections. 

Polls suggest the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) will be by far the largest party, with the CDU a distant second, and the socialist Left Party (die Linke) next in line. 

Given that the CDU refuses to join a coalition or formally "work together" with either the AfD on the right or the Left Party, this could make establishing a functioning government extremely challenging.

"With both the AfD and the Left there are such fundamental differences to the [Christian Democratic] Union, that direct cooperation is out of the question," Merz told the local Mitteldeutsche Zeitung and Magdeburger Volksstimme newspapers on Tuesday.

But Merz said that some kind of CDU-led minority government operating with support from individuals in the Left Party on a policy-by-policy basis had proven viable in other states.

"We see how it's possible to govern in Thuringia and Saxony," he said of two other eastern states where the AfD is either the strongest single party, or a close and influential second.

"But it needs to be clear that there are limits," Merz added, saying he felt these limits lay in holding Cabinet positions and formulating government policy.

Can this also work in Saxony-Anhalt?

Numerically, the parliamentary arithmetic could be more problematic in Saxony-Anhalt than any other state to date, at least based on the opinion polls prior to Sunday's vote. 

In Thuringia the CDU-led government only needs to convince one opposition politician of a policy to command a majority. In Saxony, that figure rises to 10 but there are more oppositon parties to try to woo.

Depending on Sunday's results, it's conceivable that a CDU-led minority government without the AfD or the Left Party could command fewer than 40% of the seats, or fewer still if the Greens fail to clear the 5% hurdle and enter parliament. And it would likely only have one party, the Left, to try to win over, assuming it planned to continue to exclude the AfD.

Prior to the vote, the Left in Saxony-Anhalt have said their condition would be having a more direct say on policy plans. How both sides might define this, and what compromises they might be willing to entertain once the results are in on Sunday night, remains unclear for now.

Skip next section Explosive devices discovered at substation in eastern Germany

Explosive devices discovered at substation in eastern Germany

Police have found several explosive devices near the Jänschwalde power station in the eastern German state of Brandenburg, according to media reports on Tuesday.

The devices were discovered at an electrical substation in Turnow-Preilack, southeast of Berlin, after potential damage to a power line was detected at around 8 a.m. on Tuesday, police said.

"Evidence is being secured," a police spokeswoman said. "Bomb disposal experts are on site."

Police added that there was no immediate danger to the public and that no one was hurt.

The Brandenburg state criminal ⁠police office ​has taken over the investigation of the incident.

Grid operator 50Hertz said "as yet unidentified perpetrators are believed to ​have caused damage to several power ​lines" in the transmission grid.

It added that there was a brief ‌power ​cut but all power lines were back in operation and the general electricity supply ​was never affected.

Further details were not immediately available.

The apparent attempted attack comes after several incidents targeting power supply in the greater Berlin area.

In January, suspected far-left extremists set fire to high-voltage power lines near a power station in southwest Berlin, causing power cuts to 45,000 homes.

In March 2024, a group set fire to a large electricity pylon needed to supply the Tesla factory in Grünheide near Berlin. That caused a halt in production for several days.

Skip next section German part-time jobs reach record high

German part-time jobs reach record high

The share of part-time workers in Germany reached a new high of 40.3% in the second quarter, according to analysis by the Institute for Employment Research (IAB).

The number of part-time workers increased 0.5% compared to the same period last year, to 16.936 million. At the same time, the number of full-time workers fell by 0.9% to 25.138 million.

The IAB named two reasons for the trend.

It said there had been employment growth in sectors with a high proportion of part-time work, such as health care and teaching. It also cited job cuts in sectors dominated by full-time work, such as manufacturing.

"The economy has recently stabilized, so the working hours of employees are rising slightly again," said the IAB's Enzo Weber. "But the crisis-hit manufacturing sector is losing many full-time jobs, meaning that overall fewer hours were worked."

The average weekly working hours for full-time employees remained constant at 38.32 hours in the second quarter. For part-time workers, it rose slightly to 18.88 hours.

Skip next section Germany to officially blame Russia for attempted drone attack: media reports

Germany to officially blame Russia for attempted drone attack: media reports

The German government reportedly believes a Russian intelligence service was behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport last month.

Various German media reports citing unnamed sources said Berlin would announce the details of its investigation into the incident, including the finding that Moscow was responsible, later on Tuesday.

The government has not commented on the reports, but Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt are scheduled to give a press conference on the matter in the German capital later this afternoon.

Following the discovery of an explosives-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport on August 4, Berlin referred to a "hybrid attack" and said only that "foreign powers" could be involved. Some lawmakers pointed the finger at Russia, but the government stopped short of identifying a culprit.

Media outlets also reported on Tuesday that the German government was preparing countermeasures against Moscow as part of its response. According to Spiegel, those measures could include the expulsion of Russian diplomats and the closure of Russia's consulate in Bonn.

Skip next section German union slams Volkswagen CEO over potential plant closures

German union slams Volkswagen CEO over potential plant closures

The head of the IG Metall union has warned Volkswagen's management it is making a "big mistake" by considering further layoffs and possible plant closures.

Volkswagen is already planning to cut 50,000 jobs by 2030, but the management has said more savings are needed, with the future of several factories uncertain.

In comments published in the Augsburger Allgemeine newspaper on Tuesday, union chief Christiane Benner said she would oppose any closure of the carmaker's plants in Emden, Zwickau, Hanover or Audi's Neckarsulm site at an upcoming supervisory board meeting on the cost-cutting plans.

"It is a big mistake by Volkswagen management to put the plants in Emden, Zwickau, Hanover and Neckarsulm at risk of closure, seek to cut another 50,000 jobs and at the same time announce that the operating margin must rise from 3.8% most recently to 8%-10% by 2030," Benner said.

She added that the company was required to honor commitments made to workers under an agreement reached in 2024.

Around 30,000 jobs depend on the Emden plant in northern Germany, Benner said, while the Zwickau site is particularly important for eastern Germany.

She argued there was "plenty of time to develop prospects for both sites" and said announcements about further potential cost-cutting measures had only created confusion and undermined morale among workers.

Skip next section Germany 'will not be intimidated' by Russia: Wadephul

Germany 'will not be intimidated' by Russia: Wadephul

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Berlin would offer a measured response to last month's discovery of an explosives-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport. 

The German government has not officially said who it believes was behind the August 4 incident, although there has been widespread speculation that Moscow was responsible. Russia's embassy in Berlin has denied involvement.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said an investigation into the incident was nearing completion and vowed to provide a clear-cut response in coordination with NATO and EU allies.

News outlets Welt and Politico reported on the weekend that the German government was preparing to announce that Russian intelligence was behind the attempted drone attack.

German media have reported on Tuesday that the federal government would issue an announcement later Tuesday.

When asked to comment, Foreign Minister Wadephul said Germany would not overreact and that its response would be "firm."

"Germany must position itself in such a way that anyone who attacks us knows we will respond. And we are now preparing that response carefully," he told journalists at a press conference in Algiers.

"Germany will not be intimidated in any way, and that will continue to be the fundamental stance of our policy," Wadephul said.

When asked whether Berlin should be worried about a potential counter-response from Moscow, Wadephul said: "Russia must know that Germany is a stabilizing force in Europe, one that is always prepared to negotiate, but which will not be intimidated."

Skip next section German Foreign Minister talks gas, energy supply in Algiers

German Foreign Minister talks gas, energy supply in Algiers

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul says gas from Algeria could help replenish Germany's gas storage facilities in the future.

"Diversification is absolutely the order of the day," the top diplomat told reporters in Algiers on the second day of his trip to North Africa.

Wadephul described Algeria as a "reliable partner" that was already supplying gas to EU countries Italy and Spain.

"Both in terms of securing critical raw materials and in matters of energy security, we need reliable partners and resilient supply chains, particularly in our immediate neighbourhood," the minister said.

Wadephul added that Algeria's potential as a future supplier of green hydrogen would only make the partnership more important.

Energy supply under pressure

Wadephul's visit comes at a time when the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Middle East is heaping pressure on energy supplies.

"It is quite clear that we must diversify. We need multiple sources of supply," Wadephul said.

Additionally, Germany's gas storage facilities are currently only about 50% full, with the government-mandated target of 70% by November seen as impossible to reach. Storage facilities were 67% full at the same time last year. But despite the low levels, the government has said there is no danger of a gas shortage.  

Wadephul met with Algerian Energy Minister Mohamed Arkab on Tuesday, where his focus was "trying to negotiate long-term contracts for Germany."

"If that is possible, then we will have another reliable source here, which is of course also important for our gas storage facilities," Wadephul said.

The foreign minister is traveling with an economic delegation and was also expected to meet representatives from German companies. He was also due to meet with Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune.

On Monday, Wadephul was in Tunisia where he met Head of State Kais Saied and his counterpart, Mohammed Ali Nafti.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag! from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

You join us as German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul seeks to secure gas contracts on a visit to Algeria.

The top diplomat stressed that Germany needed to diversify its energy sources at a time when the effective closure of the Middle East's Strait of Hormuz is constraining energy supply and pushing up prices.  

We're also expecting an announcement from Berlin this afternoon outlining a response to the discovery in August of a drone laden with explosives at Leipzig airport.

Meanwhile, the boss of Germany's IG Metall union has criticized the management of automaker Volkswagen for considering more layoffs and potential plant closures.

Stay with us for all these stories and more.
